title: On Internal Pendulums, Tsunamis of Urgency, and Two Life-Giving Disciplines for Educators s-for-educators
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Writing near the end of the chaotic 2019-2020 school year, Stuart describes the disorienting emotional swings of teaching through emergency remote instruction — unpredictable surges of workload and swings between encouragement and discouragement based on shifting evidence of student motivation. He names two disciplines that steady him amid this "tsunami of urgency": returning to fundamentals, by repeatedly asking what education is for and what he can and cannot control about student motivation, and committing to genuine rest, defined concretely as bounded work hours and full days off. He argues that internal disorientation distorts perception, making small tasks feel large and increasing the pull toward procrastination, which is why deliberate practices rather than willpower alone are needed to stay grounded. The piece closes by redefining professionalism itself not as constant output but as internal stability regardless of circumstance.
points: Stuart names the psychological toll of unpredictable remote-teaching workload directly, comparing himself to "an ant crawling on the beach in the shadow of a 20-foot tsunami."

His first discipline — returning to fundamentals by repeatedly asking what education is for and what is and isn't within a teacher's control — is framed as an anchor against chasing "new and innovative technique."
His second discipline is a concrete definition of rest: full 24-hour breaks from teaching and email each weekend, treated as necessary rather than optional given finite capacity.
He redefines professionalism itself as "internal stability, come what may" rather than sustained high output, a reframe aimed at teachers running on empty at the close of a disrupted school year.
quotes: Just as I think I'm getting the hang of the external and internal work of this emergency remote teaching thing, a new rush of workload that I didn't anticipate comes rushing in or I receive new information about the degree to which my students are or are not motivated.
It's all a bit disorienting. And when you're experiencing this kind of internal disorientation, your perception gets skewed. Small tasks feel big. The urge to procrastinate grows.

This return to fundamentals anchors us. It reminds us that we're not missing some new and innovative technique. It helps us retrieve the truth that our mastery of teaching is a process, not a finished product.

Rest is the complete setting down of one's work and picking up of one's avocational pursuits and life-critical relationships. It's going to bed on time. It's taking at least a full 24 hours off from teaching (and emails!) each weekend.
Committing to rest coincides with acknowledging that I am finite and that my work is a marathon and not a sprint. It recognizes that there's only so much juice in an orange.
I want to remind myself that the professionalism I'm after looks like internal stability, come what may.
